ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Methods US MTurk participants (N = 858; September 2021) engaged with real COVID-19 tweets in a simulated Twitter feed.

> Participants (N = 858) were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) during September 2021 and were compensated based on standard survey-taking rates.

> In the first section, participants were presented with a series of real tweets on controversial topics related to COVID-19, including the COVID-19 vaccine, mask usage, and hydroxychloroquine (Table 2).

> As shown in Figure 1, participants were instructed to interact with each tweet as if they were using Twitter by selecting one or more of the following options: "Like," "Reply," "Retweet," or "Quote Tweet."

> Following this simulated newsfeed exercise, participants completed a battery of questionnaires assessing individual traits and attitudes (Haupt et al., 2024).

> Participants were asked how much confidence they had in medical scientists to act in the best interests of the public.

> All models used participants with complete data on the independent variables (N = 851); 7 participants were excluded from the regression due to incomplete data.

> Another limitation is the demographic composition of the sample; being sourced from MTurk, it may not represent the broader population of Twitter users, especially considering cultural and geographical variations in social media (Buhrmester et al., 2011).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Methods US MTurk participants (N = 858; September 2021) engaged with real COVID-19 tweets in a simulated Twitter feed.
Participants (N = 858) were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) during September 2021 and were compensated based on standard survey-taking rates.

In the first section, participants were presented with a series of real tweets on controversial topics related to COVID-19, including the COVID-19 vaccine, mask usage, and hydroxychloroquine (Table 2).

As shown in Figure 1, participants were instructed to interact with each tweet as if they were using Twitter by selecting one or more of the following options: "Like," "Reply," "Retweet," or "Quote Tweet."
Following this simulated newsfeed exercise, participants completed a battery of questionnaires assessing individual traits and attitudes (Haupt et al., 2024).
Participants were asked how much confidence they had in medical scientists to act in the best interests of the public.
All models used participants with complete data on the independent variables (N = 851); 7 participants were excluded from the regression due to incomplete data.

Another limitation is the demographic composition of the sample; being sourced from MTurk, it may not represent the broader population of Twitter users, especially considering cultural and geographical variations in social media (Buhrmester et al., 2011).

text.text: Psychological traits and social identities have been linked to misinformation sharing, but most studies measure passive or low-effort engagement.
Less is known about high-effort engagement that requires users to write a response.

We examined whether cognitive reflection, motivated reasoning variables (political orientation, religiosity, trust in medical scientists) and personality traits are differentially associated with liking, retweeting, replying to, and quoting COVID-19 misinformation and public-health-unaligned tweets.
Methods US MTurk participants (N = 858; September 2021) engaged with real COVID-19 tweets in a simulated Twitter feed.
Replies and quotes were manually coded as endorsive or combative.
We fit OLS regressions for each engagement type (N = 851) and estimated relative importance using Shapley (LMG) decomposition of R².
Endorsive replies and quotes were rare (7.3% and 4.3% of participants for misinformation).

Political conservatism and religiosity were associated with endorsive misinformation replies, and motivated reasoning variables were the largest contributors in all reply and quote models, though these models explained little variance (adjusted R² ≤ .03).
Cognitive reflection was negatively associated only with liking, and grandiose narcissism was the largest contributor to retweeting.
Conclusion Classical reasoning, personality and motivated reasoning explanations of misinformation propagation were each supported, depending on the type of engagement.
Simulation tasks that measure multiple engagement behaviors can help clarify inconsistent findings in the misinformation literature.
Circulation of misinformation on social media has become a critical concern, especially during public health crises like the COVID-19 pandemic.
Misinformation is defined as unverified rumors and false claims that spread widely and deceive audiences (Kumar & Geethakumari, 2014).

text.text: In addition to misinformation, we also examine engagement with posts that express unsafe public health practices with regard to COVID-19, even if they do not make an explicit false claim.

We classify these tweets as public health guideline "Unaligned" (hereby referred to as just "Unaligned") if they did not contain misinformation but still expressed sentiment that was not aligned with public health guidelines.

Unlike misinformation, which contains a discrete, verifiably false claim, unaligned tweets do not make falsifiable factual assertions; instead, they express skepticism, dismissiveness, or opinion-based rhetoric which promoted harmful practices during the pandemic.
Examples of guideline unaligned tweets include expressing negative stances towards wearing a mask, toward vaccines, or a positive stance towards using hydroxychloroquine to treat COVID-19.

This distinction follows broader work cautioning that not all content contributing to public misperception is straightforwardly false or fabricated but can still promote distrust in public health guidance through framing, selective emphasis, or misguided opinions (Jack, 2017).

Another explanation for how misinformation spreads is the motivated reasoning account.
This view holds that people evaluate information according to pre-existing goals, choosing to endorse and share content that fits those goals (Kahan, 2015; van der Linden, 2022).

In addition to political identity, other social factors could evoke motivated reasoning.

Trust in information sources is one such factor: if people fundamentally distrust authorities or medical experts, they may be more inclined to believe fake news and misinformation or conspiracy theories.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, for instance, individuals with low trust in medical scientists and public health institutions were observed to be more susceptible to conspiracy theories about the virus (Hunt et al., 2022).

Though prior work suggests various potential predictors of misinformation engagement and propagation, the relative contributions of these factors have not been studied together extensively.

The present research aims to fill this gap by systematically investigating individual factors (e.g., classical reasoning, motivated reasoning, psychological traits) associated with different types of engagement behaviors on social media (e.g., reply).

Participants (N = 858) were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) during September 2021 and were compensated based on standard survey-taking rates.
The survey was administered via Qualtrics and divided into two primary sections.

text.text: Input text responses were required for "Reply" and "Quote Tweet" selections.
This design aimed to simulate real-world engagement behavior with social media content.

We further manually categorised replying and quoting as endorsive (positive sentiment/ agreeing with original tweet) vs non-endorsive (negative sentiment/disagreeing with original tweet) replies or quotes, with endorsive/affirmative interactions suggesting misinformation propagation, while non-endorsive interactions were actually corrective in nature, and minimized misinformation propagation (and are therefore not explored in this paper).

Each reply and quote was coded separately for each tweet, and the endorsive reply and quote outcomes are the number of replies (or quotes) to misinformation or Unaligned tweets that were coded as endorsive.
Following this simulated newsfeed exercise, participants completed a battery of questionnaires assessing individual traits and attitudes (Haupt et al., 2024).

text.text: The present study examined the role of psychological and social factors in predicting high effort forms of misinformation engagement.

Taken together, the findings offer a nuanced picture of how individual differences shape the ways in which people interact with misinformation online, extending the work of Haupt et al. (2024) to high effort engagement behaviors.

text.text: On average, participant replies and quotes counts for all tweets were lower than the like and retweet counts, suggesting that not many users are willing to exert the effort needed to write responses.

Overall, the main explanations for misinformation propagation were each supported, depending on the type of engagement: classical reasoning (CRT) was an inhibitor of passive engagement (liking), personality (grandiose narcissism) was associated with low-effort active engagement (retweeting), and motivated reasoning variables were most associated with high-effort active engagement (replying and quoting).
CRT was significantly negatively associated with liking Unaligned tweets, and was a large contributor to the model based on Shapley-weighted variance.
This pattern suggests that lower reflective thinking is a meaningful driver of passive misinformation endorsement.

This is in-line with previous literature that indicates that individuals who lean towards quickheuristic thinking are more susceptible to misleading content (Haupt et al., 2024; Munusamy et al., 2024).

text.text: However, no other form of Unaligned engagement was significantly associated with CRT.
Thus, H1 is only partially supported for liking Unaligned tweets (passive engagement).
CRT was not associated with endorsive replies or quotes to misinformation or Unaligned tweets.
Thus, H2 is not supported.

This finding suggests that higher cognitive reflective thinking may not reduce high-effort active engagement with misinformation; individuals who choose to author a reply may already spend more time deliberating on the tweet, regardless of their reflective nature (Pennycook et al., 2016).

text.text: Notably, CRT was negatively associated only with liking; it was not associated with retweeting, or with endorsive replying or quoting.
In contrast, political orientation and religiosity were the largest contributors to endorsive replying to misinformation (see Motivated Reasoning).

This suggests that the reflective-thinking account (Pennycook & Rand, 2019 , 2021) may best explain quick, low-effort judgments such as liking, while endorsements that users write themselves may depend more on pre-existing beliefs and group identity (Kahan, 2015).

Political orientation did not significantly predict liking or retweeting Unaligned tweets; thus, H3 is not supported.
However, political conservatism was positively associated with endorsive replies and quotes to misinformation and was the largest contributor to both models, partially supporting H4.

This is consistent with prior work suggesting that partisan identity alignment can increase susceptibility to misinformation consistent with one's worldview (Bayrak et al., 2025; Lois et al., 2026; Rhodes, 2022; Spohr, 2017; Van Bavel & Pereira, 2018; Weeks, 2015).

text.text: There was no significant association between grandiose narcissism and high effort engagement.

These findings suggest that those higher in covert tendencies may be more likely to write responses despite the higher efforts, whether or not they agree with the tweet, while those with grandiose tendencies may be more averse to high effort responses and prefer low effort propagation.

A strength of our study was our distinction between passive engagement, low-effort active engagement, and high-effort active engagement metrics.
As evidenced by many variables discussed, there were significant differences in how these engagement types differed across variables.
For example, CRT was only associated with liking, while motivated reasoning variables contributed the most to replying and quoting, and grandiose narcissism to retweeting.

Another strength of this study was the fact that we manually distinguished between positive replies (and quotes) (endorsive active engagement) and negative replies (and quotes) (non-endorsive active engagement) to misinformation and Unaligned tweets.

A strength and limitation of this study is the use of a simulation exercise rather than using real interactions on Twitter/X. While a simulated newsfeed exercise allows for measurement of engagement behaviors aligned to true Twitter interface (which may be better than simple Likert-type questions), it still lacks ecological validity as participants' interactions with tweets might be altered as their engagement behaviours are not reflected on their actual public profile.

Another limitation is the demographic composition of the sample; being sourced from MTurk, it may not represent the broader population of Twitter users, especially considering cultural and geographical variations in social media (Buhrmester et al., 2011).

This study extends prior work on misinformation propagation by moving beyond passive and low-effort active engagement to examine how classical reasoning, motivated reasoning, and psychological factors shape high-effort active engagement (replying and quoting) with both misinformation and public-health-unaligned content.

The findings highlight that engagement type matters: classical reasoning, motivated reasoning, and personality traits did not operate uniformly across passive, low-effort active, and high-effort active behaviors, and in several cases (e.g., CRT, openness, grandiose narcissism, political orientation) their effects on higheffort engagement differed from their established effects on liking and retweeting, even from the previous paper linked to this study (Haupt et al., 2024).

text.text: Motivated reasoning variables, rather than CRT, contributed the most to high-effort engagement, suggesting that findings based mainly on passive engagement may not extend to replying and quoting.

By measuring multiple engagement behaviors, we found that classical reasoning, personality and motivated reasoning explanations of misinformation propagation were each supported depending on the type of engagement, suggesting that simulation exercises measuring multiple engagement types can help clarify disparities in the misinformation literature.

Future work that can investigate different misinformation user types, examine social media data from naturalistic settings, and test differential responses to user-specific interventions will be necessary to translate these psychological and behavioral distinctions into practical tools for reducing misinformation propagation.
